cognate: *h₂wes- 'spend (the night), stay' + *nókʷt- in the accusative of duration: ON vera (vesa) + nótt; Gk ἰαύω / ἄεσα + νύκτα(ς); Ved. vas- + rātrim (night-word renewed). In the pivot and the two Homeric anchors a negated *swep- word follows: ON mátti ekki sofa ~ Gk ἀΰπνους.
drift_or_renewal: ON vera has become the suppletive copula, but with an accusative of time ('var þessa nótt', 'váru þar eina nótt') it keeps the old sense 'stay over, spend the night'. Vedic renews the night word with rātri-. The Greek negation is an adjective (ἀ-υπνος) where ON has a clause (mátti ekki sofa).
shared_syntax: verb *h₂wes- + accusative of duration *nókʷt-; then a sleep word with negation saying the night was sleepless
context: A man spends a night (or nights) awake because of trouble: Njáll lies awake at Þórolfsfell; Achilles (Il. 9.325) and Odysseus (Od. 19.340) say they spent sleepless nights. Both are personal narrative of a hero's worry or hardship.
phrase: *nókʷtm̥ h₂wes- 'spend the night', here 'spend a sleepless night'
note: Recalled: LIV gives *h₂u̯es- 'verweilen, übernachten' with Gk ἄεσα / ἰαύω and Ved. vásati; 'spend the night' as a core sense is from the literature. I would defend the verb + night collocation (Greek, Vedic and ON corpus hits) more strongly than the sleeplessness add-on, since lying awake at night is a universal motif. The ON is saga prose, and the 'stay over' use of vera is everyday idiom.

cognate: ON ljós n. 'light', here 'world (of the living)', and Ved. loká- m. 'world', both from *lewk- 'bright, open' (different derivatives: *leuk-s- vs *lowkó-). Each is used with a near-deictic: í þvísa ljósi ~ asmin loke 'in this world'.
drift_or_renewal: Different derivatives of one root, each reaching 'world'. In ON it is 'light' used for the world of the living; in Indo-Iranian it is 'free space'. The other member is renewed: ON í ǫðru 'in the other' against Ved. parasmin / amuṣmin (loke) 'in the further / yonder (world)'.
shared_syntax: locative of the *lewk- noun with 'this', set against 'the other / further' world: a two-world merism
context: Both are ritual-legal formulas about where a man's standing will hold. Njáll's saga has the court oath 'so help me God in this light and the other'. AV 15.12 says whether the offerer's abode (āyatana) stays in this world, and AV 6.117.3 asks to be debt-free in this, the further and the third world.
phrase: 'in this world and the other' with a *lewk- word for 'world'
note: Low: the ON oath is Christian and could render Latin 'in hoc saeculo et in futuro', so only the word choice ljós for 'world' would be inherited. The Vedic two-world idiom (ayáṃ loká / asaú loká) is recalled. The root equation is secure, but the derivatives are not the same word.

near_miss.lead: lét illa í svefni eina nótt ~ ἀΰπνους νύκτας ἴαυον
near_miss.why_not: Shares night + sleep only. 'Tossed in his sleep one night' is not the 'spend a sleepless night' phrase and has no *h₂wes- verb. Counted only as context for the claim on BS-071d1.
The bundle's partners (Il. 11.10, 6.389, Thuc., Hdt.) have nothing to do with it. The pivot is cited only as support for the BS-071d1 sleepless-night claim.
'Cold are women's counsels' is a Norse proverb. Cato's gelidam (of timber) shares only the *gel- root, with no matching context.

near_miss.lead: kin-term pairs (athair ar a mac ⁊ māthair ar ingin ~ πατήρ τε θυγατρὶ παῖς τε μητρὶ; genealogies)
near_miss.why_not: Pairing kin terms is generic, and the genealogies are lists. The Irish (hiding from father/mother) and Greek (incest) contexts differ. Il. 22.239 πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ is the only formula, and it has no partner of the same shape.

near_miss.lead: weapons gleam (blika ~ блестеть, *bʰleyǵ-) with/like the sun (*sóh₂wl̥)
near_miss.why_not: The image of weapons gleaming in the sun is generic. The syntax differs: in ON the sun shines on the shields; in the bylina the sword gleams 'like the sun', a simile. The bylina is a late text. The cognacy of блестеть with blika is plausible, but on its own it is not enough.
There are no shared wordings. 'ann henni sem augum í hǫfði sér' (in the context) is a good formula, but nothing in the bundle matches it.

near_miss.lead: eigi fellr tré við it fyrsta hǫgg ~ πρῶτος ... δουρὶ τυπεὶς
near_miss.why_not: The match of first + *dóru + struck is chance: δόρυ means 'spear' and the context is a killing, not a felled tree. The ON proverb belongs to a widespread medieval proverb type (Lat./Ger. 'one stroke does not fell an oak'), which is probably not inherited.

near_miss.lead: í andliti sem blóð ... fǫlr sem gras ~ aevi florem
near_miss.why_not: blóð ~ flos share at most a root (*bʰleh₃-), with no phrase in common. 'Pale as grass' recalls Sappho 31 χλωροτέρα δὲ ποίας, but the words are not cognate and Sappho is not in the corpora (searched ποία: no hit). A thematic parallel only.
'Kneel before (submit to)' and Plautus' list of body parts share only the knee word.
ON 'you have struck me so near the heart' (an emotional injury) and AV 'the vigour in your hearts' share only *ḱḗr. The syntax and figure differ.

error.evidence: 'segja frá Kára at hann ...'; context after: 'heyrði at Kári vakti'

note: Second reading of 14 flagged bundles. 2 claims: the sleepless night *nókʷt- + *h₂wes- (medium), and 'this world' with a *lewk- word, ON ljós ~ Ved. loka (low). 10 near-misses, 1 error.
